Question ten. What is PCA, and what does it do? Principal component analysis finds the directions of greatest variance, each at right angles to those before, and projects the data onto the first few, to compress, plot or decorrelate it. On the page's ten scaled features, two components keep forty-two percent of the variance, and the last two keep none: two of the columns are combinations of others. The trap is that variance isn't signal. In this simulation, the first component holds ninety-seven percent of the variance, and predicts the label barely better than a coin flip. The other three percent predicts it at ninety-one. PCA never sees the label. One model only goes so far. Next, many.

Question eleven. What are ensembles? Explain bagging and boosting. Bagging trains models independently, each on a bootstrap sample, and averages them, mainly cutting variance. Boosting trains them in sequence, each correcting the last, mainly cutting bias, and it overfits unless regularized. Averaging has a floor: adding models cuts the variance only down to a level set by how correlated their errors are.

Question twelve. How does a random forest differ from a single decision tree? It bags trees, and at each split lets a tree consider only a random few features: here, eight of the sixty-four pixels of handwritten digits. One tree scores eighty-four percent. Each forest tree is weaker than a plain bagged tree, seventy-six percent against eighty-two, but their mistakes overlap less, so together they score ninety-eight against ninety-six.
